newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to sell "Stinger" missiles to S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to sell "Stinger" missiles to S.Korea.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it planned to sell 1,065 shoulder-fired "Stinger" anti-aircraft missiles and 213 launchers to South Korea for $307 million.

The Pentagon told Congress that Seoul was seeking the Stingers for defence against any attack from North Korea. The sale, expected to be completed without objection from Congress, would be the first transfer of the little arms to the South.

Stingers, fired by a single soldier with the launcher resting on a shoulder, find and track targeted aircraft or helicopters after launch. They are made by the Hughes Missiles System Co., a unit of General Motors Corp..

"This is the first sale of 'Stinger' missiles to Korea and it will enable the Korean Army to develop a defence capability with an ability to protect itself from unwarranted aggression from the air as well as enhance its inter-operability with U.S. forces," the Pentagon said in an announcement.
Such major foreign military sales require scrutiny by Congress but the plan is expected to be completed without opposition.
The United States has 37,000 of its troops stationed in South Korea in a region that has remained one of the world's most tense since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce.

While Washington and Seoul are close allies, there has been some recent tension between their defence departments over the possibility that the South might buy heavy Russian-made SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles fired from fixed sites.

Defence Secretary William Cohen has instead urged Seoul to buy heavy U.S.-built Patriot anti-aircraft missiles which can be used against both attacking aircraft and tactical ballistic missiles such as Scuds, which are in the North Korean arsenal.

Although the little Stingers are highly effective and accurate at short ranges and relatively low altitudes, they would not take the place of heavier missiles such as the SA-12 or Patriot in an overall defence scheme.

The United States has voiced concern about the inter-operability of Russian-made weapons with U.S. aircraft in any new Korean war, fearing that the Russian arms might accidentally shoot down American planes which they are not programmed to avoid.
